description: A vendor exposed personal health information due to an unauthorised cloud bucket
A company reused mobile location data for targeted advertising without consent
An adult video streaming site’s open database exposed ~11 billion user records including names, emails, chat logs, IPs, sexual orientations, etc., risking phishing and blackmail
root_cause: Misconfigured Elasticsearch server left publicly accessible without a password. No evidence of misuse reported at breach time.

description: The largest breach ever: hackers in 2013 stole data for all Yahoo accounts (names, emails, hashed passwords, etc.). Initially reported as 1 billion, later updated to 3 billion. Security Q&A and other data were compromised, raising identity theft risk.
root_cause: Hacking by a state-sponsored actor (per Yahoo) in 2013. Yahoo faced criticism for late disclosure (2016) and had to force password resets. Passwords were hashed; no payment info stolen.

description: A March 2018 revelation that India’s entire Aadhaar biometric ID database was exposed. Personal details (names, Aadhaar numbers, bank info, etc.) of over a billion citizens were being sold online. Even biometric data (photos, fingerprints, iris scans) were accessible.
root_cause: Data leak via partner: A state-owned utility’s system was unsecured, allowing outsiders to pull Aadhaar data. Lack of robust access control on the Aadhaar database enabled this massive privacy breach.

description: In mid-2022, a hacker on a forum claimed to have stolen ~23 TB of data from Alibaba’s servers, including names, government ID numbers, phone numbers, addresses and even police records. It reportedly included a Shanghai police database hosted in Alibaba’s cloud, sparking outrage.
root_cause: Server left unprotected: Critical Alibaba Cloud databases had no password, allowing easy access. Alibaba was criticized for lax security despite sensitive government info on its cloud. Previous scraping incidents showed ongoing security negligence.

description: A major real-estate title insurance firm leaked 16+ years of mortgage and title records (~885 million files). Exposed data included bank account details, Social Security numbers, wire transactions, etc.. Fortunately, no reports of malicious use emerged despite the exposure.
root_cause: Website design flaw: A configuration error allowed anyone to access documents by changing a URL parameter. The records were sequentially numbered, so no authentication was needed to view others’ files.

description: Email marketing firm Verifications.io exposed a database containing 763 million unique email addresses and other personal data (names, phones, birthdates, genders, etc.). The data sat publicly visible, putting hundreds of millions at spam and phishing risk.
root_cause: Unsecured MongoDB: The company left a MongoDB instance openly accessible without a password. This lack of basic security meant anyone could query and copy the data. No hacking needed – just an open door.

description: In mid-2021, a user database for ~700 million LinkedIn members was posted for sale on a hacker forum. The leaked data included email addresses, full names, phone numbers, geolocation, job histories, genders, and more. About 92% of all LinkedIn users were affected.
root_cause: Data scraping via API: Attackers exploited LinkedIn’s API and scraped user info, violating terms of service. LinkedIn claimed no private data was taken (it was publicly viewable info), but the aggregation was a major privacy violation.

description: In April 2019, security researchers found two public Facebook app datasets exposed on the internet – one from Mexican media firm Cultura Colectiva – containing 533 million Facebook records (comments, likes, account names, IDs, etc.). The data was later leaked for free in 2021, including phone numbers for millions of users, posing significant privacy risks.
root_cause: Third-party negligence: Two Facebook third-party app developers stored user data on open servers without protection. Facebook IDs and activity info were exposed. Facebook hadn’t detected it until researchers (UpGuard) reported it.

description: Separate from Yahoo’s 2013 mega-breach, Yahoo was hit by a second breach in 2014 affecting 500 million user accounts. Stolen data included names, emails, phone numbers, birthdates, hashed passwords, and some security questions (unencrypted). Yahoo disclosed this in 2016.
root_cause: Nation-state hacking: Yahoo said a “state-sponsored actor” hacked its network in 2014. The breach went undetected for years. Yahoo knew of some intrusion in 2014 but failed to investigate fully, only disclosing after stolen data appeared for sale online.

description: Marriott disclosed in Nov 2018 that its Starwood Hotels subsidiary had been infiltrated since 2014. Data on ~500 million hotel guests was stolen – including names, contact info, passport numbers, travel itineraries, and ~100 million payment cards (encrypted). It’s one of the largest breaches of personal info by a nation-state.
root_cause: Long-term espionage: Hackers (allegedly China’s state security) had persistent access to Starwood’s network for 4 years. The breach began before Marriott acquired Starwood (2016) and was only discovered in 2018.

description: In Oct 2016, hackers stole 20 years of data from AdultFriendFinder and related adult sites (412 million user accounts). Exposed info included usernames, emails, and passwords – 99% of which were hashed with the weak SHA-1 and were quickly cracked. The breach outed many users of these adult sites, posing serious privacy and reputational harm.
root_cause: Hacking + weak encryption: Attackers exploited Friend Finder Networks’ poor security. Passwords were stored with obsolete SHA-1 hashes (unsalted), which allowed ~99% to be cracked in days. Essentially, the sites failed to properly secure user credentials.

description: In June 2013, MySpace (once a top social network) was breached, exposing ~360 million user accounts. Data included usernames, email addresses, and passwords. It wasn’t publicly revealed until 2016, when the data was being circulated among hackers. Many passwords were weak or reused, putting other services at risk.
root_cause: Hack by criminals: A Russian hacker gained MySpace’s user database. MySpace had not discovered it at the time. Once exposed, MySpace invalidated all pre-2013 passwords to mitigate further misuse.

description: In June 2018, a security researcher found a publicly accessible database belonging to Exactis (a marketing/data aggregator) containing ~340 million individual records. The data included extremely detailed personal profiles on hundreds of millions of Americans (e.g. phone numbers, addresses, interests, ages of children).
root_cause: Unsecured database: Exactis stored this massive dataset on a server without any password or firewall, open to the internet. Anyone could query millions of Americans’ personal details – a glaring security failure by the firm.

description: In May 2018, Twitter disclosed a glitch that had exposed user passwords in an internal log in plain text. Every Twitter user (330 million at the time) was urged to change their password. Twitter said no breach or malicious use was detected, but the incident underscored the risk of insider exposure.
root_cause: Software bug: Twitter’s hashing mechanism failed and wrote passwords in plaintext to an internal log file. Although only employees could see the log, it violated security best practices. Twitter quickly fixed the bug and found no evidence of misuse, but treated it seriously.

description: Chinese tech giant NetEase (operator of 163.com email) reportedly suffered a breach in Oct 2015 affecting about 234 million user accounts. Email addresses and plain-text passwords were purportedly stolen, though NetEase never emphatically confirmed the breach’s details. Many Chinese users had to change credentials.
root_cause: Hacking: Exact details aren’t public, but the data appeared on underground forums in 2016. Users confirmed some passwords were valid. The lack of hashing for passwords indicates poor security and enabled attackers to directly obtain login credentials.

description: In Jan 2021, Chinese social media firm Socialarks exposed an ElasticSearch database of ~200 million scraped social media profiles from Facebook, Instagram, and LinkedIn. Exposed data included names, contact info, profile descriptions, follower counts, etc. Even though data was aggregated from public profiles, the compilation at this scale posed privacy issues.
root_cause: Unsecured ElasticSearch: The server was left open (no password or encryption) on the public internet. Essentially, anyone who knew the IP could query the data. This was a case of careless cloud configuration rather than an active hack.

description: In June 2017, a GOP consultant (Deep Root Analytics) left a database of ~198 million U.S. voter records exposed online. Personal voter information (names, addresses, birthdates, party affiliation) plus analytic data on political preferences were accessible to anyone. This represented the majority of U.S. voters and was one of the largest voter data leaks in history.
root_cause: Cloud misconfiguration: The voter data (1.1 TB) was stored on an Amazon S3 bucket without any access restriction. UpGuard researchers discovered the open repository. The trove included not just basic voter rolls but predictive models on voting behavior, all left unprotected.

description: In Oct 2013, an identity thief posing as a private investigator gained access to a massive database of U.S. consumers held by Court Ventures (an Experian subsidiary). He illicitly obtained ~200 million records including credit card and Social Security numbers, which were then sold to criminals engaged in identity theft.
root_cause: Social engineering: The hacker tricked Experian’s subsidiary by posing as a legitimate client from Singapore. Staff were convinced to give him query access to the internal database. This deception went undetected, illustrating a failure in verifying customers of a data broker.

description: In June 2012, LinkedIn was breached, but the full extent (over 165 million accounts) wasn’t revealed until 2016. Initially only ~6.5 million password hashes leaked, but hackers actually stole a much larger dataset including ~117 million unsalted SHA-1 password hashes. This data resurfaced in 2016, forcing widespread password resets and compromises on other sites (via reused passwords).
root_cause: Hacking: Hackers exploited LinkedIn’s defenses in 2012 (possibly via an SQL injection or stolen admin creds). LinkedIn only notified the public of 6.5 M leaked hashes then. In 2016, the breach data was found being sold, exposing LinkedIn’s failure to investigate thoroughly. Passwords weren’t salted, making cracking easier.

description: In Dec 2018, popular lip-sync app Dubsmash was hacked, resulting in ~162 million user records stolen. Data included usernames, email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords. In early 2019, the Dubsmash data appeared for sale on the dark web alongside other breaches, indicating it was likely sold to or obtained by various hackers.
root_cause: Hacking – credential theft: Attackers likely exploited Dubsmash’s servers in late 2018 (exact vector not disclosed publicly). The stolen data was later sold on a darknet marketplace for Bitcoin. Dubsmash forced password resets, but the breach highlighted risks for smaller apps integrated with social media.

description: In Oct 2013, Adobe Systems suffered a breach of ~153 million customer accounts. Hackers stole account data including usernames, email addresses, encrypted passwords, and password hints (in plaintext). Because the password encryption was weak and many hints were obvious, millions of passwords were quickly cracked, leading to credential-stuffing attacks on other services.
root_cause: Hacking: Cybercriminals breached Adobe’s network (possibly via a server vulnerability) and exfiltrated the user database. Adobe encrypted passwords but without salt, and stored hints in plaintext – a serious design flaw. The breach was discovered when hackers leaked the data online. Adobe had to notify users and offered credit monitoring.

description: In Feb 2018, the popular diet/exercise app MyFitnessPal (by Under Armour) was hacked, exposing 144–150 million user accounts. Compromised data included usernames, emails, and hashed passwords (older ones SHA-1, newer ones bcrypt). No financial info was affected, but users had to change passwords, and the data later circulated on hacker forums.
root_cause: Hacking: Attackers exploited MyFitnessPal’s systems in early 2018 (exact method not disclosed publicly). The breach wasn’t detected until a few weeks later. Under Armour had hashed the passwords (transitioning to stronger bcrypt), which limited damage. The incident still underscored the risks of large user-data troves in fitness apps.

description: One of the most damaging breaches: credit bureau Equifax announced in Sept 2017 that personal data of ~148 million Americans (and others) had been stolen. The data was highly sensitive – names, Social Security numbers, birthdates, addresses, and in some cases driver’s license numbers and credit card info. This exposure of nearly half the U.S. population’s identities led to widespread fear of identity theft.
root_cause: Unpatched software: Hackers exploited a known Apache Struts web-server vulnerability that Equifax had failed to patch. The attackers had months-long access to Equifax’s network. Equifax’s poor security practices (no encryption for much data, missed patches) enabled the massive theft. The breach led to the CEO’s resignation and a $700 M settlement.

description: In May 2014, eBay revealed hackers had breached its network, compromising 145 million user records. Stolen data included names, emails, addresses, phone numbers, and encrypted passwords. Users were forced to reset passwords. No financial data (stored separately) was taken, but the breach still raised concerns due to eBay’s size.
root_cause: Credential compromise: Attackers obtained a small set of eBay employee login credentials, which allowed database access. The intrusion happened in Feb–Mar 2014 and went unnoticed for weeks. This breach highlighted the risk of weak internal controls and the need for better employee authentication and network segmentation at eBay.

description: In May 2019, online design platform Canva suffered a breach impacting ~137 million users. Exposed information included names, usernames, email addresses, city, and passwords hashed with bcrypt. The hacker (alias “GnosticPlayers”) bragged about the attack to the media and provided evidence of the data. Canva notified users and reset passwords for safety.
root_cause: Hacking (credential theft): The hacker gained access to Canva’s databases; Canva said they detected the attack and stopped it, but not before data was taken. The attacker also claimed to have OAuth tokens for users logging in via Google. Canva’s quick user notification and strong password hashing mitigated damage, but the breach showed even creative-tech firms are targets.

description: In 2008, Heartland Payment Systems (a major card payment processor) was hacked, exposing ~130 million credit and debit card numbers. This breach, revealed in early 2009, was the largest credit card theft at that time. The stolen card data led to tens of millions in fraudulent charges and forced Heartland to pay over $140 M in fines and settlements.
root_cause: SQL injection attack: Hackers led by Albert Gonzalez exploited a known SQL vulnerability in Heartland’s network to install malware that stole card data. Heartland, which processed 100 M transactions a month, failed to detect the data exfiltration. The incident pushed industry-wide adoption of end-to-end encryption and tokenization in card processing.

description: In July 2018, marketing data firm Apollo left a massive store of personal data exposed publicly. The dataset contained billions of data points on businesses and individuals; about 126 million unique email addresses were found in HaveIBeenPwned from this leak. Data included names, email, employers, job titles, locations, etc., aggregated from various sources – a treasure trove for spammers and phishers.
root_cause: Unsecured database: Apollo failed to secure a repository of combined data it had gathered (likely an open MongoDB or SQL database accessible without auth). A portion of the data was later shared with breach-notification services. The incident underscored privacy risks posed by data brokers compiling large profiles and not safeguarding them.

description: In June 2013, a hack of social/dating network Badoo resulted in ~112 million user records being circulated in hacker forums. Leaked data included names, birthdates, email addresses, and password hashes (MD5). Badoo users potentially faced account takeovers (if they reused passwords) and privacy issues from exposure of dating profiles.
root_cause: Hacking: The Badoo breach details are sparse, but likely involved an attacker gaining database access in 2013. The data was found online in 2016, suggesting Badoo either didn’t detect it or didn’t disclose it promptly. Passwords were stored with unsalted MD5 hashes, a weak practice that made cracking trivial. This breach highlighted common security lapses in mid-2010s social sites.
potential_causes: a hack of social/dating network badoo

description: In July 2019, Capital One revealed a hacker stole data on ~100 million U.S. customers and 6 million Canadians. Exposed data included names, addresses, ZIPs, phone numbers, emails, birthdays, and self-reported income; about 140k Social Security numbers and 80k bank account numbers (U.S.), plus ~1 million Social Insurance Numbers (Canada) were also taken. The breach raised serious concerns about cloud security.
root_cause: Cloud misconfiguration: A former AWS employee exploited a misconfigured Capital One AWS S3 bucket and firewall to obtain the data. The hacker, Paige Thompson, found credentials in a server that allowed access to the cloud storage. Capital One’s failure to properly secure its AWS instances and detect exfiltration was blamed. This case became a landmark warning about securing cloud infrastructure.

description: Online invitation service Evite suffered a data breach around 2013, but it only came to light in April 2019 when stolen Evite data was found for sale. Approximately 101 million user records were affected. Exposed data included names, usernames, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, dates of birth, and passwords (stored in plaintext or weakly encrypted).
root_cause: Hacking & long-term unnoticed: Hackers accessed Evite’s user database back in 2013, but Evite was apparently unaware until the data appeared on the dark web in 2019. Alarmingly, many passwords were stored unhashed (in plain text), a fundamental security failure. This incident shows breaches can remain hidden for years if companies lack monitoring.

description: In December 2018, Quora announced that hackers had accessed data of about 100 million users. The stolen information included account names, email addresses, hashed passwords, and all non-anonymous content (questions, answers, comments) posted by users. Anonymous postings were not affected. The breach threatened user privacy, as content that users tied to their accounts could be correlated and sensitive Q&A activity exposed.
root_cause: Hacking (malicious third party): Quora’s investigation suggested a malicious actor gained unauthorized access to one of its systems. Details weren’t publicly shared, but could involve exploiting a vulnerability or stolen credentials. Quora logged out all users and invalidated passwords. The breach highlighted that even well-known platforms can be compromised by determined attackers.

description: In early 2012, Russia’s largest social network VK (formerly VKontakte) was hacked, exposing 93.6 million user credentials. Email addresses, usernames, and plaintext passwords were leaked. The data became available on the dark web in 2016, indicating that VK’s breach went undetected or unreported for years. Users of VK (popular across CIS countries) had to change passwords and many experienced spam or account hijacks.
root_cause: Hacking & poor storage: Attackers breached VK’s systems and were able to obtain the user database. VK stored passwords in plain text or weakly hashed, as evidenced by the leaked data. This made the breach extremely damaging (no cracking needed). The incident underscored the importance of proper password hashing – a lesson that came too late for VK’s millions of users.

description: MyHeritage, a genealogy and DNA testing service, was breached in Oct 2017 (disclosed June 2018) affecting 92 million users. A security researcher found a file containing MyHeritage emails and hashed passwords on a private server. Fortunately, no DNA or raw genetic data was leaked – only account info – and MyHeritage reported no malicious use. They still required password resets for all users.
root_cause: Hacking (undisclosed vector): The exact attack route wasn’t revealed, but MyHeritage’s security team confirmed an unknown party “exfiltrated” the user email & hash database. They praised their own response in identifying and disclosing the breach promptly. The passwords were hashed (with salt), and the company added two-factor authentication after the incident.

description: In Dec 2016, Chinese video streaming site Youku (often called China’s YouTube) was reported to have suffered a breach exposing 92 million user accounts. Data included email addresses and unsalted MD5 password hashes. The breach wasn’t widely publicized outside China, but the data set eventually leaked online, putting users (especially those reusing passwords) at risk.
root_cause: Hacking: Likely part of the wave of 2016 credential breaches, attackers stole Youku’s user database. The use of unsalted MD5 for passwords made it easy for hackers to crack a large portion of them. Alibaba (Youku’s owner) forced password resets. This breach illustrated that even major platforms in China faced the same security challenges as global ones.

description: In Feb 2014, Russian portal Rambler (akin to Yahoo) was breached, and ~98 million user accounts’ data was stolen (later reported as ~90M unique). Usernames (which often were the email prefix @rambler.ru) and plaintext passwords were leaked. When the data surfaced in 2016, it caused an uproar as none of the passwords were encrypted, highlighting a massive security lapse.
root_cause: Hacking & plaintext storage: Hackers infiltrated Rambler’s user database in 2014. The company had been storing passwords in clear text, an egregious practice. Thus, the breach directly exposed credentials, leading to immediate compromise of accounts. The incident forced Russian services to reevaluate their password storage policies.

description: A data misuse (not a traditional hack) in which a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, obtained personal data of ~87 million Facebook users without consent. A third-party personality quiz app harvested data not only from 270k users who installed it, but also from tens of millions of their unwitting friends, due to Facebook’s lax API at the time. CA used this data for targeted political advertising in the 2016 US election and Brexit campaign, causing a global privacy outrage.
root_cause: Platform loophole & abuse: Developer Aleksandr Kogan’s app exploited Facebook’s then-permissive API to collect friends’ data, which he sold to Cambridge Analytica in violation of Facebook’s policies. Facebook knew its API allowed expansive data access but did not audit misuse until the scandal erupted. This event led to Facebook tightening data sharing and facing $5 B FTC fines for privacy violations.
potential_causes: facebook’s lax api at the time

description: In October 2016, video-sharing site Dailymotion was hacked, exposing about 85 million user accounts. Data included usernames and email addresses, and about one-third of the accounts had password hashes (bcrypt) leaked. Dailymotion forced a reset for those with compromised passwords. The breach had potential to lead to account hijacks on Dailymotion or other sites if users reused credentials.
root_cause: Hacking: Details remain scarce publicly, but security researchers suspect credential stuffing or exploiting an outdated vulnerability could be to blame. Fortunately, Dailymotion had protected passwords with bcrypt, limiting immediate damage. The company disclosed the breach promptly after discovery, an example of better practice in breach response.

description: The largest healthcare breach in US history: in Feb 2015, health insurer Anthem was hacked, exposing personal information of 78.8 million individuals. Compromised data included names, birthdates, member IDs, Social Security numbers, addresses, phone numbers, emails and employment info. Medical records weren’t directly taken, but the data was highly sensitive. Anthem paid substantial fines ($115 M settlement) and it raised alarms about healthcare data security.
root_cause: Spear-phishing & state actors: The breach originated when a single employee at an Anthem affiliate opened a malicious phishing email, giving attackers a foothold. Advanced hackers (suspected Chinese group) then moved laterally, accessing Anthem’s data warehouse. Notably, Anthem had not encrypted SSNs in the database, drawing criticism. The attack went undetected for weeks as data was exfiltrated.

description: In mid-2012, cloud storage company Dropbox was breached, with ~68.7 million user credentials stolen. The breach wasn’t fully revealed until 2016 when the database leaked. Data included email addresses and hashed passwords. Dropbox initially knew of a smaller breach (usernames/passwords posted online in 2012) but did not realize the scale. When the full extent emerged, Dropbox forced password resets for all affected accounts.
root_cause: Hacking via reused creds: It’s believed attackers used credentials from the LinkedIn 2012 breach to access a Dropbox employee’s account, which contained a project file with user passwords. Half the passwords were hashed with SHA-1 (now considered weak) and half with stronger bcrypt. Dropbox improved security afterward (added two-factor auth), but the delay in discovery highlighted challenges in breach detection.

description: In 2013, blogging platform Tumblr was breached, exposing ~65 million user accounts’ information (primarily email addresses and passwords). However, Tumblr didn’t disclose it at the time. The breach became public in 2016 when the data was found for sale. Fortunately, Tumblr had salted-hash protected the passwords (SHA1+salt), so they were not easily crackable. Tumblr notified users and required password resets once it learned of the incident.
root_cause: Hacking: The exact method remains unknown, but likely an attacker found a vulnerability in Tumblr’s infrastructure in 2013. Tumblr’s strong password hashing meant the dumped credentials weren’t immediately useful, but users who reused passwords elsewhere were still at risk. The incident was among several “long tail” breaches only revealed years later, underscoring that breaches can hide until the data surfaces publicly.

description: In late 2016, ride-hailing company Uber was breached: hackers stole data on 57 million riders and drivers. Personal info included names, emails, phone numbers of 50M riders, and about 600k U.S. drivers’ license numbers. Uber infamously paid the hackers $100k under the guise of a “bug bounty” to delete the data and didn’t disclose the breach until a year later, sparking outrage and regulatory penalties.
root_cause: Credential compromise: Two hackers obtained Uber’s AWS login credentials from code Uber had inadvertently posted on GitHub. Using these keys, they accessed Uber’s cloud servers and extracted the data. Uber’s decision to pay off attackers and hide the incident was widely condemned; it led to firings and legal action. The breach highlighted the importance of securing developer credentials and responding transparently.

description: In Sept 2014, Home Depot announced hackers had planted malware on its in-store payment system, resulting in 56 million credit/debit card numbers being stolen over five months. Additionally, 53 million customer email addresses were taken. It was one of the largest retail card breaches, slightly bigger than Target’s. Home Depot had to pay banks and card brands ~$180 M and faced customer lawsuits.
root_cause: Malware via third-party: Attackers gained network access through a Home Depot vendor’s stolen credentials, then installed custom point-of-sale malware on Home Depot’s registers. The malware, masquerading as antivirus, siphoned card data until discovery. Lack of network segmentation and weak authentication for vendors were key factors. Home Depot invested heavily in security improvements after.

description: Discount retailer TJX (TJ Maxx, Marshalls, etc.) was hit by a series of intrusions from July 2005 to Jan 2007, compromising at least 45.6 million payment card numbers. The hackers (the same ring as Heartland/Target) stole card magstripe data from store payment systems over many months. Personal info of ~450k customers (drivers license numbers, etc.) was also stolen. The breach cost TJX ~$170 M and was a watershed moment for retail cybersecurity.
root_cause: Wardriving & weak Wi-Fi: Hackers led by Albert Gonzalez breached a Marshall’s store’s Wi-Fi, which was using outdated WEP encryption, to gain network access. They then installed sniffer malware to capture card data. TJX’s failure to encrypt card data and use stronger wireless security allowed the breach. It was one of the first major retail breaches to spur PCI security standard updates.

description: Over the 2013 holiday season, Target was breached, with attackers stealing ~40 million customers’ credit/debit card details and personal info (names, addresses, emails, phone numbers) of ~70 million people. The breach occurred from Nov–Dec 2013 and was disclosed in Dec. It caused huge fallout: banks reissued cards, Target’s CEO resigned, and the company incurred ~$292 M in costs (after insurance).
root_cause: Third-party intrusion: Hackers broke in through a HVAC contractor’s stolen network credentials to Target’s vendor portal. From there, they installed POS malware on Target’s checkout systems, which silently harvested card swipes. Target had missed alerts from its security systems about the unusual activity. This breach became a case study in supply-chain security vulnerabilities.

description: In July 2015, hackers calling themselves “Impact Team” breached Ashley Madison – a dating site for married people – and stole data on ~32 million users. They released multiple dumps of sensitive user information: names, emails, physical addresses, profile details (including sexual preferences), and seven years of credit card payment records. The leak exposed many users (including public figures), leading to divorces, extortion attempts, and reportedly some suicides.
root_cause: Hacktivist attack: The attackers claimed they easily penetrated Ashley Madison’s poorly secured network. They demanded the site shut down or they’d release data. When the parent company refused, the hackers published the data on the dark web. Investigations showed the site’s security and data retention practices were inadequate (e.g., some ‘deleted’ profiles were included), amplifying the fallout.

description: In Aug 2022, password-manager LastPass suffered a serious breach. Hackers stole encrypted password vaults and other customer data, potentially impacting ~30 million users. The attackers first breached a developer’s account, then later obtained a backup of customer vault data. If users had weak master passwords, their stored site passwords could be cracked. This breach undermined trust in password managers and prompted urgent user guidance to change all vault passwords.
root_cause: Advanced persistent threat: Attackers targeted a LastPass DevOps engineer with a complex attack, bypassing multi-factor auth to compromise their laptop. They then accessed LastPass cloud storage. LastPass admitted to failures in segmentation and notified users to beware of phishing. The vaults were encrypted (except URLs), so vault contents remain secure if the master password was strong and not reused.

description: In Aug 2022, streaming media software company Plex announced that a hacker had accessed its user database, affecting most of its ~20 million users. Compromised data included usernames, emails, and passwords (hashed with best practices). Financial info was not stored by Plex. Users were forced to reset passwords. The breach raised concern since Plex is often linked to smart TVs and other devices.
root_cause: Unknown vulnerability: The exact entry point wasn’t disclosed; Plex said it fixed the method used. All passwords were hashed and salted (Plex didn’t specify algorithm, likely bcrypt). Plex’s swift reset of all accounts limited damage. The incident highlighted that even smaller, “behind the scenes” services can be targets for credential theft.

description: In Jan 2021, men’s clothing retailer Bonobos had a database hacked, exposing 7 million customer shipping addresses, 1.8 M account details, and 3.5 M partial credit card records (no CVV). The combined ~12.3 M records were later dumped on a hacker forum. Some password hashes (SHA-256) were cracked (158k), though the majority were stronger SHA-512 that held. Personal details and order info were included, posing a privacy and fraud risk.
root_cause: Backup server compromise: The attacker claimed to have breached a Bonobos backup database that was left accessible. Bonobos said its production systems weren’t directly touched – suggesting a cloud backup or dev environment was the weak link. The incident underscores that backups containing live data must be as secure as primary systems.

description: In Feb 2020, MGM Resorts confirmed that personal details of ~10.6 million former hotel guests were found on a hacker forum. The data (dating back years) included names, postal addresses, phone numbers, emails, and birthdates of guests – including celebrities, tech CEOs, government officials, etc. No financial data or passwords were leaked. The exposure raised concerns about targeted scams against high-profile individuals.
root_cause: Unauthorized access: The data likely came from a breach of an MGM third-party server or cloud database in 2019. MGM stated no payment info was taken and notified affected guests. This incident highlighted how hospitality data (guest lists) can be lucrative for attackers (targeting VIPs for spear phishing). It also showed that companies must secure not just payment info but any personal data collected.

description: In Sept 2022, Optus (Australia’s #2 telecom) was hacked, exposing data of 9.8 million customers. Stolen information included names, dates of birth, phone numbers, email addresses, and for some, physical addresses, driver’s license or passport numbers. The hacker demanded a ransom and when unpaid, leaked ~10k records. The breach sparked government criticism and fast-tracked reforms to how ID documents are used for customer verification in Australia.
root_cause: API left open: The attackers reportedly accessed an unsecured API endpoint that didn’t require authentication. This API provided customer data directly. Essentially, Optus had a publicly accessible interface exposing subscriber info. Such a basic security oversight in a major telco shocked many and demonstrated the importance of securing APIs.

description: In Oct 2022, health insurance giant Medibank was hit by a cyberattack. Hackers stole ~200 GB of data on 9.7 million past and present customers, including sensitive health claim information. Data included names, birth dates, passport numbers, and details of medical procedures/diagnoses. The criminals tried to extort Medibank and ultimately dumped files (which they crudely indexed as “good” and “naughty” based on diagnoses), causing public distress and government intervention.
root_cause: Stolen credentials & ransomware: Attackers used credentials obtained on the dark web to access Medibank’s internal systems. Once in, they ran a script to exfiltrate data at scale. Medibank had no cyber insurance and refused to pay the ransom, leading to the data leak. The breach highlighted the dire need for robust access controls and encryption of health data.

description: In May 2020, budget airline EasyJet revealed hackers had breached its systems, accessing ~9 million customer records. Email addresses and travel details were taken, and in a more limited subset (~2,200 customers), credit card details (including CVV) were stolen. The attack had gone undetected for months. Under GDPR, the UK ICO investigated, and EasyJet faced potential fines. Customers were warned of phishing risks.
root_cause: Sophisticated cyber-attack: EasyJet described the attack as “highly sophisticated”, possibly by state actors or well-organized cybercriminals. It might have been an exploitation of a known vulnerability or a targeted spear-phishing of an admin. The precise method wasn’t publicly disclosed. The incident underscored that airlines, with rich personal and payment data, are prime targets.

description: In Nov 2020, stock image marketplace 123RF had 8.3 million user records stolen and offered on a hacker forum. Data included names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, PayPal emails, IPs, and hashed passwords (MD5). Researchers confirmed many hashes were easily cracked to plaintext passwords. No financial data was stolen, but the personal info and weak password hashes posed risks to users (account takeover, phishing).
root_cause: Hacking: Attackers breached 123RF’s systems (perhaps via an old unpatched CMS or reused cred). They extracted the user database. The company acknowledged the breach after data appeared online. Notably, MD5 hashing was used for passwords, which is insecure – many were decrypted by security researchers. Post-breach, 123RF had to improve its security and user notification practices (under watch by regulators from multiple countries).

description: In Oct 2021, an anonymous leaker posted a 125 GB torrent containing virtually all of Amazon Twitch’s source code and creator payout data. The leak included internal AWS infrastructure code, an unreleased Steam competitor, and earnings of top streamers. While user accounts (and payment info) weren’t directly compromised according to Twitch, the incident was a massive intellectual property breach and raised concerns about possible injection of malware via source code leaks.
root_cause: Server misconfiguration: Twitch admitted a “server configuration change” left an internal system exposed, allowing a third party to access data without authorization. The attacker wasn’t financially motivated (posted data free) but rather aimed to “foster disruption” and criticize Twitch’s community. The breach highlighted the need for rigorous cloud config reviews and internal monitoring. Twitch rotated all streaming keys and bolstered security after.

description: In March 2020, Marriott reported another breach (distinct from the 2018 Starwood incident): ~5.2 million hotel guests’ information was accessed. The data (names, addresses, emails, phone, birthdays, loyalties, room preferences) was obtained using login credentials of two employees at a Marriott franchise. No payment card or passport data was taken. This second hit to Marriott’s reputation in two years underscored ongoing security challenges.
root_cause: Stolen credentials: Attackers likely obtained valid login info for a third-party hotel chain employee (possibly via phishing or reused passwords). Using those credentials, they accessed guest info for weeks before detection. Marriott stated it has since enhanced monitoring and multiple auth for franchise partners. The incident underlined that insiders and partners are often the weakest link for hotel data security.

description: In Sept 2021, luxury retailer Neiman Marcus disclosed an “unauthorized party” accessed 4.6 million customer accounts, including names, contact info, account passwords, and even payment card numbers (with expiration dates) for ~3.1 million cards. Fortunately, 85% of the cards were expired or invalid. The breach had gone unnoticed since it occurred in May 2020. Neiman Marcus offered free credit monitoring to customers.
root_cause: Hacking (undetected): The attackers likely exploited the website or an application vulnerability in 2020 to siphon out the customer database. The breach was only found in 2021 during system upgrades. The incident highlighted the importance of continuous security audits. It also served as a reminder from Neiman’s 2014 smaller breach – indicating perhaps lessons weren’t fully learned, as password reuse could endanger customers across sites.

description: In Jan 2021, a niche dating site MeetMindful was breached by the ShinyHunters hacker group. Data on ~2.3 million users was dumped on a dark web forum. The dump included full names, email addresses, city, body details, dating preferences, marital status, birthdates, IP addresses, Facebook auth tokens, and bcrypt-hashed passwords. Private messages were not compromised, but the exposed profile data was sensitive and potentially embarrassing.
root_cause: Hacking & data dump: ShinyHunters likely exploited MeetMindful’s web application (they’re known for attacking startups) and stole the user database. They then freely posted the data online, possibly for reputation rather than profit. The breach was devastating for a small dating service, illustrating that even minor sites hold data attractive to hackers – and that robust hashing (bcrypt) is essential but doesn’t protect public-facing profile info.

description: In Jan 2021, ShinyHunters also leaked ~1.9 million user records from Pixlr, a popular online photo editing app. The data (which was stolen in the same incident as 123RF, Pixlr’s parent company) contained email addresses, usernames, countries, and hashed passwords. The information was dumped publicly on a forum. Users of Pixlr were advised to change passwords, and the incident showed that even seemingly small apps can expose millions of accounts.
root_cause: Piggy-back breach: Pixlr’s data was compromised via the 123RF breach – the attacker got Pixlr user info when they breached 123RF’s shared infrastructure. The company hadn’t segregated data between services. ShinyHunters then published the Pixlr data alongside 123RF’s. The case emphasizes the importance of isolating systems of acquired or related services to prevent one breach from cascading into another.

description: In Oct 2021, four sister e-commerce sites (Tackle Warehouse, Running Warehouse, Tennis Warehouse, Skate Warehouse) disclosed a breach impacting ~1.8 million customers collectively. Hackers accessed customer names, addresses, account passwords, and full credit/debit card numbers with CVVs. The breach occurred around mid-Oct and was revealed by a law firm in Dec 2021. It’s notable for the theft of complete card info, which is highly sensitive.
root_cause: Web skimming or DB breach: The specifics weren’t disclosed, but the breach likely involved an injection of malware on the checkout pages or a database compromise, given card data and plaintext (or reversibly encrypted) card numbers were obtained. The companies said they did not know if card data was hashed or not. This incident highlights the ongoing threat of Magecart-style attacks on online stores and the need for PCI compliance.

description: In Feb 2022, Harbour Plaza (a HK hotel chain) was breached, with ~1.2 million guest records stolen. The data came from hotel reservation databases and potentially included personal guest info and credit card details (though the company wasn’t sure if the hackers decrypted the card data). Local authorities were alerted, and customers were advised to monitor financial statements.
root_cause: Hacking: The breach likely occurred via an exposed application or compromised credentials into the hotel’s reservation system. Harbour Plaza said it couldn’t confirm if encrypted credit card data was decrypted by the attackers. This uncertainty underscores a common issue: companies often don’t know the full extent of what attackers accessed or could do if encryption keys were also stolen.

description: In Nov 2021, high-end jeweler Graff was hit by Conti ransomware, with hackers stealing data on its wealthy clientele. Over 69k documents (invoices, receipts, client lists) were stolen – including personal details of celebrities and world leaders like Donald Trump, David Beckham, Oprah, and Gulf royals. When Graff refused to pay a $15 M ransom, Conti leaked ~11k files (~1% of the data) as proof and threatened more leaks. The incident raised fears of high-profile blackmail.
root_cause: Ransomware infiltration: Conti hackers penetrated Graff’s network (possibly via a phishing email or vulnerable remote access), exfiltrated sensitive client data, then deployed encryption. The double-extortion tactic meant even if Graff restored systems, the data theft remained an issue. The breach highlighted that luxury brands are targets not just for financial gain but also for the sensitive secrets of the ultra-wealthy. Graff eventually had to acknowledge the breach publicly due to the leaked VIP names.

description: In Sept 2022, the Los Angeles Unified School District (second-largest in the US) was hit by a ransomware attack (Vice Society group) over Labor Day weekend. The attack disrupted IT systems for 1,000+ schools and exposed ~500 GB of data after LAUSD refused to pay. Leaked data included employee Social Security numbers, student records (addresses, disciplinary notes, psychological assessments), health and COVID vaccination data, and other sensitive files. The breach raised alarms about cybersecurity in K–12 education.
root_cause: Known vulnerabilities ignored: Prior to the attack, federal agencies had warned LAUSD of critical vulnerabilities in its systems, but the district hadn’t fully addressed them. Vice Society exploited these weaknesses (often by phishing or via unpatched servers) to encrypt systems and steal files. The incident illustrated the severe impact of ransomware on public institutions and the importance of heeding security advisories.

description: In April 2020, as Zoom usage soared, hackers obtained ~500,000 Zoom account credentials and either sold or freely posted them on the dark web. These weren’t from Zoom’s own systems being breached, but rather login-email/password pairs gathered from earlier breaches of other services and tried against Zoom (“credential stuffing”). Many people re-used passwords, so hackers could log into those Zoom accounts – in some cases joining meetings or accessing recordings.
root_cause: Credential stuffing: Attackers leveraged login info from older breaches (dating as far back as 2013) to see which Zoom accounts they unlocked. Users who reused passwords were compromised. This led to incidents of “Zoom-bombing” and privacy issues in meetings. Zoom invalidated the breached passwords and implemented rate-limits and other measures to curb such attacks. This episode underscores not a failure of Zoom’s infrastructure per se, but of password re-use by consumers and the resulting cascade effect across services.

description: In Feb 2020, a white-hat hacker tried to warn Slickwraps (a phone case skin retailer) of a severe security hole and was ignored. Another hacker saw the blog post and exploited the flaw, then emailed all 370k customers announcing the breach. Exposed data included names, emails, addresses, and transaction histories (no passwords or payment info). The breach was especially humiliating because customers learned of it directly from the hacker’s mass email.
root_cause: Ignored warnings -> exploit: Slickwraps had a known vulnerability (likely an open API or database) that a researcher publicly highlighted after the company ignored private reports. A second hacker then easily breached the “abysmal” defenses and demonstrated it by emailing customers. Essentially, lack of a security response process turned a potential quiet fix into a very public breach. The incident is a cautionary tale on responding to security research.

description: In Apr 2020, Fortune 500 healthcare provider Magellan Health was hit by a sophisticated phishing-and-malware attack. Attackers accessed login credentials via malware on an employee’s computer, then infiltrated a corporate server, ultimately deploying ransomware. The breach compromised ~365,000 individuals’ data, including names, contact info, employee IDs, Social Security numbers and W-2 tax details.
root_cause: Phishing & malware: The attack was multi-stage – first a malware email to steal an employee’s credentials, then using those to impersonate a client and phish further internally. After gaining broader access, the hackers launched ransomware. The incident shows how attackers combine social engineering with technical exploits in healthcare, and it cost Magellan tens of millions to remediate.

description: In April 2020, Nintendo announced ~160,000 Nintendo Network IDs had been compromised, and by later investigation the number nearly doubled to 300,000. The attackers used these accounts to fraudulently purchase digital goods. Exposed information included names, birthdates, countries, and email addresses associated with the accounts. Nintendo forced password resets and urged users to enable 2-factor authentication.
root_cause: Credential stuffing: Nintendo believed hackers obtained accounts by trying login credentials stolen from other breaches (the Nintendo IDs were legacy accounts often reusing passwords). Many victims admitted to password reuse. Nintendo did not find evidence of a direct breach of their servers. This event pushed many in the gaming community to stop reusing passwords and to use 2FA, given how lucrative gaming accounts can be (stored payment methods, game assets).

description: In Sept 2020, email marketing firm Mailfire (serving adult dating and e-commerce sites) was breached, exposing notification data from over 70 websites. The exposed database (320 M records) included names, ages, genders, locations, IP addresses, profile photos, and private chat messages from users of various adult dating sites. It also inadvertently revealed many fake profiles used on these sites (as the data included evidence of scam bot accounts).
root_cause: Unsecured ElasticSearch: Mailfire left an ElasticSearch server of message logs publicly accessible, which a hacker discovered. No password or firewall protected it, so the attacker could query all data in real-time. This not only breached user privacy but also exposed shady practices (fake profiles) by some Mailfire clients. The incident underscores the risks when B2B service providers don’t secure the data they handle for clients.

description: In Mar 2020, Brazilian biometrics firm Antheus Tecnologia had its fingerprint database hacked. Hackers accessed ~2.3 million raw fingerprint data points representing 76,000 unique fingerprints. They also stole ~81.5 M records of personal data (email addresses, employee phone numbers, admin login details). The fingerprint data could potentially be reverse-engineered to recreate original fingerprints, raising alarm as biometric breaches are irreversible (you can’t change your fingerprints).
root_cause: Hacking: Attackers targeted an insecure server at Antheus, known for fingerprint tech used by government and private clients. The stolen fingerprint data was in a format that, while not images, contained enough info to reconstruct prints. This breach highlighted the high stakes of biometric data storage – and prompted calls for stronger protection (e.g., encryption and template-only storage) for biometric info. Brazilian authorities took notice given the sensitivity and the company’s government ties.

description: The SolarWinds Orion incident (disclosed Dec 2020) was a landmark supply-chain attack. Hackers (likely Russia’s APT 29) compromised SolarWinds’ software build system and inserted a backdoor (“Sunburst”) into Orion network management updates released in March–June 2020. ~18,000 public and private organizations installed the tainted updates. The attackers then selectively used this backdoor to infiltrate U.S. government agencies (Treasury, DHS, etc.) and companies (Microsoft, FireEye). It was called the biggest cyber-espionage attack in U.S. history.
root_cause: Compromised software update: Attackers breached SolarWinds’ development environment and altered a DLL in the Orion product, signing it with SolarWinds’ certificate. When customers updated, they unknowingly opened a backdoor. The true “breach” was of multiple organizations’ networks via this trusted channel. This campaign went undetected for months. It led to a U.S. executive order on improving software supply-chain security, as the traditional security tools failed to catch this subtle but far-reaching attack.

description: In Mar 2022, a SafetyDetectives report revealed Turkey’s Pegasus Airlines had an open AWS S3 bucket that exposed 6.5 TB of sensitive data. Over 23 million files related to the airline’s Electronic Flight Bag (EFB) system – including flight charts, navigation materials, crew info, and plaintext credentials/secret keys – were publicly accessible. The leak raised concerns about aviation security (pilots’ apps and airline operations) and whether any bad actors quietly harvested data before it was secured.
root_cause: Open cloud storage: Pegasus Airlines had misconfigured its AWS cloud storage, leaving it publicly readable. The bucket contained not only flight operation files but also ~400 files with plaintext passwords and secret keys for various systems. Although Pegasus said they found no evidence of misuse, it’s possible data was stealthily exfiltrated. The incident underscores how a single cloud permission mistake can jeopardize critical infrastructure.

description: In Jan 2022, hackers breached the Philippines’ COMELEC (Commission on Elections) servers, reportedly stealing ~60 GB of sensitive data related to the upcoming election. The data supposedly included admin credentials, voter personal information, and even PINs of vote-counting machines. Such information could potentially be used to undermine election integrity. The government initially downplayed the extent, but the “Comeleak” incident revived memories of a 2016 breach when the entire voter database was leaked.
root_cause: Election system hack: Details are confidential, but it appears the attackers penetrated the COMELEC network (possibly via phishing an IT staff or exploiting a web app). They claimed to have enough to “map the full election infrastructure”. This breach, coming just months before national elections, highlighted the high stakes of election cybersecurity. It pressured officials to audit and fortify systems (and led to some denying that machine PINs were valid to reassure the public).

description: In April 2022, Mailchimp, a large email marketing provider, was breached via social engineering. Attackers fooled Mailchimp support staff to gain access to ~100 client accounts, specifically targeting crypto companies. Notably, they accessed the mailing list of Trezor (a hardware crypto wallet) and sent all its users a fake “security update” email that was actually a phishing link. Some users entered their recovery seeds on the fake site, leading to their crypto wallets being emptied.
root_cause: Insider targeted: The attackers conducted a social engineering attack on Mailchimp employees, tricking them into giving access to internal tools. With those tools, they exported client email lists. This is an example of “hack the helper” – instead of hacking Trezor directly, they hacked its email provider. Mailchimp acknowledged the breach and improved its security, but the incident shows how a third-party service breach can cascade into a highly targeted phishing campaign.

description: In Feb 2005, data broker ChoicePoint announced it had inadvertently sold the personal records of ~145,000 people to identity thieves. Fraudsters set up fake accounts to pose as legitimate small businesses and bought extensive consumer reports from ChoicePoint. Data included names, addresses, Social Security numbers, credit reports and more. At least 700 cases of identity theft (financial fraud, etc.) were traced to this lapse. The scandal spurred the first U.S. data breach notification laws.
root_cause: Lax verification & oversight: ChoicePoint failed to vet new customers – the criminals simply lied about their identities and ChoicePoint gave them access to its databases. The breach wasn’t a hack; it was a business process failure. It only came to light due to a 2003 California law requiring notification. ChoicePoint had even earlier incidents (in 2002) but hadn’t notified victims, showing a pattern of minimal transparency.

description: In May 2006, an analyst at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs had his home burglarized, and a laptop + external drive were stolen. Unfortunately, these devices contained unencrypted personal data on 26.5 million veterans and military personnel. The data included names, birthdates, SSNs, and some disability ratings (which indicate medical conditions). The VA waited until late May to inform affected individuals, causing public outcry. The devices were eventually recovered and the FBI indicated the data hadn’t been accessed.
root_cause: Insider negligence: A VA employee had been taking work data home for 3 years with permission, but the data was not encrypted. The loss revealed VA’s “F” grade security practices. Multiple failures occurred: the employee promptly reported the theft, but VA leadership wasn’t alerted until weeks later. The breach catalyzed legislation to mandate better protection of veterans’ data and spurred government-wide security reforms (e.g., encrypting sensitive data on laptops).

description: In Oct 2007, the UK government’s tax agency (HMRC) lost in transit two CDs containing the entire Child Benefit database – personal details of ~25 million people (7.25 M families). The data included names, addresses, birthdates, National Insurance (social security) numbers, and bank account info of all recipients (basically half the UK population). The unencrypted discs were sent via ordinary mail and never arrived. This colossal blunder put millions at risk of identity fraud and rocked public confidence in government data handling.
root_cause: Operational blunder: A junior HMRC official, breaching all protocols, burned the data to CDs and sent them through untracked internal mail (TNT courier) to the National Audit Office. The package wasn’t registered and vanished. Critically, HMRC included sensitive bank and personal data that the Audit Office hadn’t even requested. The fallout included the resignation of the HMRC chairman and urgent reforms: encryption of citizen data in transit, stricter access controls, and a rethink of the upcoming national ID card plans (this breach “nailed the coffin” for public support of a central ID database).

description: In Nov 2007, Facebook launched “Beacon,” an ad system that automatically broadcast users’ outside activities to their Facebook friends (e.g. purchases on partner sites) without clear consent. For example, buying a product on Overstock.com could post an update on your Facebook feed. Users and privacy advocates erupted when surprise messages (“[User] bought X!”) spoiled gifts and revealed sensitive info. Over 50 million Facebook users were affected by default until Beacon was modified. The backlash was one of the first major privacy scandals Facebook faced.
root_cause: Design choice (opt-out default): Beacon was opt-out, meaning it shared data unless a user explicitly blocked each instance. Many didn’t know it was happening – an essential failure to obtain informed consent. MoveOn.org and 50k users protested in a “Stop Invading My Privacy” group. Within a week, Facebook backed down: Zuckerberg apologized and allowed a per-site opt-out (later Beacon was shut down entirely in Sept 2009, and Facebook settled a class-action lawsuit). This episode highlighted how even non-breach privacy harms can damage trust and led to today’s norms around clearer app permissions.

description: A major media scandal: the British tabloid News of the World was found to have illegally hacked the voicemails of hundreds of people – royalty, celebrities, politicians, and even a murdered teenage girl – in pursuit of scoops. In Dec 2011, London police said they had confirmed at least 803 phone hacking victims (and identified ~5,500 potential targets in the investigator’s notes). Reporters would call victims’ cellphone voicemail boxes using default PINs or other tricks to listen to private messages. Revelations of this practice (which dated back to early 2000s) caused public outrage, the 168-year-old newspaper’s shutdown, executive jailings, and a public inquiry into press ethics.
root_cause: Intentional intrusion: News of the World journalists and hired private investigators exploited lax security in cellphone voicemail systems – many people didn’t change default PINs, or the carriers had vulnerabilities. By dialing into voicemail remotely and entering default or guessed PINs, they accessed messages. The paper’s management initially denied widespread hacking, but evidence showed it was routine and even covered up. The harm was highly personal – e.g. deleting voicemails on a missing 13-year-old’s phone giving her family false hope. The scandal led to the Leveson Inquiry and strengthened UK privacy laws (and a hefty £20M payout to victims by Murdoch’s company).

description: In April 2011, security researchers discovered that iPhones were storing a hidden file containing a detailed log of the device’s locations over the past year. This “consolidated.db” file, which recorded cell tower and Wi-Fi hotspot positions, was unencrypted and backed up to any computer the phone synced with. The public was alarmed that Apple devices appeared to be “tracking” users’ movements. Although Apple denied it was actively tracking individuals, the data could reconstruct a user’s travel patterns fairly precisely. This raised global privacy concerns and questions from regulators.
root_cause: Software bug / design: Apple explained that iPhones were not supposed to retain a year’s worth of location cache – it was a bug that the cache wasn’t trimmed and that it continued even with Location Services off (a bug in iOS). Apple quickly released an iOS update reducing the cache to 7 days and encrypting it. They stated the data was used to quickly assist location services (AGPS) and was never transmitted to Apple without consent. The incident led to greater transparency from Apple about location data and set the stage for today’s more robust privacy controls in iOS.

description: In Feb 2010, Google launched “Buzz,” a social networking feature within Gmail. By default, Buzz automatically used a Gmail user’s contacts to create a public social network of followers/following. This meant that a user’s most-emailed contacts could be exposed on their public Buzz profile without clear permission – e.g. journalists’ confidential sources or an individual’s doctor/lawyer could be revealed as top contacts. The backlash was immediate; users felt betrayed that private Gmail relationships were made public. Google was hit with FTC charges and a class-action lawsuit over Buzz’s deceptive privacy design.
root_cause: Auto-opt-in design: Google opted everyone in to Buzz and treated Gmail contact lists as public social connections without adequate notice or consent. Many users didn’t realize this until they saw their network displayed. Within days Google scrambled to change Buzz to an opt-in model. The FTC later found Google deceived users and violated privacy promises. In Mar 2011, Google settled with the FTC, agreeing to 20 years of independent privacy audits – the first such penalty on a major tech company. Buzz was shut down in late 2011. The case is a landmark in U.S. privacy enforcement, underscoring that privacy by design (and user consent) is a must.

description: In 2019–2020, it came to light that a startup, Clearview AI, had scraped over 3 billion face images from the internet – social media, websites, etc. – to build a massive facial recognition database. They then sold access to this database to law enforcement agencies, allowing police to identify people from photos. This happened without the knowledge or consent of the individuals or the platforms. Essentially, Clearview put most of the world into what critics call a “perpetual police line-up”. The revelation sparked international outrage, lawsuits, and regulatory orders (e.g. it’s been fined or declared illegal in several countries) for violating privacy on a vast scale.
root_cause: Data scraping & repurposing: Clearview’s CEO admitted the company had scraped over 30 billion images from sites like Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, etc., often bypassing or violating those sites’ terms. They matched images to names by processing public profiles. While not a “breach” by hackers, it was an unprecedented privacy intrusion – taking public data but using it in a way users never expected (highly accurate face recognition). Clearview argued First Amendment rights to public info, but regulators deemed personal biometric data needs consent. The incident highlights the gray zone of web-scraped data: technically public, but when aggregated, hugely privacy-impacting.

description: In 2014, it emerged that Uber employees had a tool called “God View” which allowed them to see the real-time location of Uber riders and drivers on a map. Uber staff used it to casually track politicians, celebrities, and even personal acquaintances. A particularly egregious case: Uber’s NYC general manager tracked a BuzzFeed reporter’s Uber ride without her permission and greeted her by saying he was watching her approach. At a party, Uber displayed God View on a screen, showing VIPs’ movements to attendees. These revelations showed Uber’s disregard for user privacy at the time.
root_cause: Insider abuse: There was no external breach – it was Uber’s internal system lacking proper access controls. Corporate employees widely had access to rider data via God View. Uber’s policies nominally forbade unauthorized tracking, but they weren’t enforced until journalists exposed the practice. The fallout: Uber had to tighten data access, implement an ethics code, and it suffered reputational damage. This case illustrates that even absent hacking, employees can violate privacy if data isn’t locked down on a need-to-know basis.

description: In Dec 2014, a woman in Delhi was raped by her Uber driver – a horrific crime. But Uber’s response included a shocking privacy violation: Uber’s President of Business (Asia Pacific), Eric Alexander, obtained the victim’s confidential medical records from Indian police and shared them with CEO Travis Kalanick and others. They reportedly sought to discredit the victim’s story, suggesting it might be fabricated by a competitor (a baseless conspiracy). This “stunning violation of privacy” only came to light in 2017. Uber fired the executive after press inquiries, but by then the damage to Uber’s culture and reputation was done.
root_cause: Deliberate privacy intrusion: A senior Uber executive intentionally and illegitimately accessed someone’s medical rape exam records – an absolute breach of privacy and trust. This wasn’t a hack; it was a willful act likely via personal contacts or bribery within law enforcement. The rationale was doubly offensive: to spin a narrative that undermined a victim. The incident underscored a toxic culture at Uber and led to greater scrutiny of its privacy practices and internal ethics. It reinforced that privacy isn’t just about cyber security – it’s also about how companies handle extremely sensitive personal information.

description: In May 2018, an Amazon Echo device (Alexa) in Oregon recorded a private conversation between a husband and wife about hardwood floors and sent the audio to a random person on their contact list without consent. The family only found out when the recipient (an employee of the husband) called saying “Unplug your Alexa, you’re being hacked!”. The incident ignited fears that “smart speakers are eavesdropping on us” and was a PR nightmare for Amazon’s Echo, which had sold tens of millions of units. Amazon confirmed the event and called it an “extremely rare occurrence.”
root_cause: Mistaken wake + command: Amazon’s investigation found Alexa misheard background talk as a series of commands: it woke up (mis-triggered by a word sounding like “Alexa”), then caught “send message” in conversation, then a name that matched a contact, then heard confirmation (“right”). In short, an improbable chain of false triggers led Alexa to record and send the chat. Amazon quickly updated Alexa’s software to reduce such chances even further. While not a malicious breach, this highlighted the privacy trade-offs of voice assistants and prompted calls for audible indicators whenever recording is happening.

description: In 2015, smart TV maker Vizio was caught secretly collecting what its customers were watching on their TVs – second-by-second, across channels, streaming, DVDs, etc. – and selling that data to advertisers. This affected 11 million TVs sold since 2010. The viewing data was combined with third-party data (via IP address matching) to link it to individuals’ demographics (age, income, marital status, etc.). Vizio never told users it was doing this; the setting was hidden under an ambiguous name. In 2017, the FTC fined Vizio $2.2 M and ordered it to stop unauthorized tracking. It was a landmark case treating viewing data as “sensitive” information.
root_cause: Feature abuse (undeclared): Vizio enabled a feature called “Smart Interactivity” on its TVs by default, pitched as providing program suggestions. In reality, it was content recognition software scanning everything on screen and phoning home viewing logs. The feature description never mentioned data collection. Users essentially were never asked for consent. This was a deliberate design to monetize user data. The FTC deemed it unfair and deceptive. The case stands as a warning to IoT and smart device makers that surreptitious data collection will draw regulatory wrath.

description: In April 2016, an anonymous whistleblower (internally called “John Doe”) leaked 11.5 million confidential documents from Mossack Fonseca, a Panama-based law firm specializing in offshore shell companies. The “Panama Papers” exposed financial secrets of hundreds of politicians, celebrities, and business leaders across 200+ countries – revealing tax evasion, money laundering, and corruption. The leak involved ~2.6 TB of data spanning the 1970s–2015, including emails, bank account info, passport scans, and shell company records for ~214,000 offshore entities. It was likely the largest data leak in journalism history, leading to resignations of heads of state and global reforms on tax transparency.
root_cause: Insider breach: A Mossack Fonseca employee or contractor secretly copied the firm’s entire digital archive over time. They contacted a German newspaper (Süddeutsche Zeitung) in 2015 and provided the trove (encrypted). The leak was not a hack by outsiders, but an internal whistleblower breach motivated by “income inequality” and justice (as the leaker stated). Technically, Mossack Fonseca also had very poor IT security – outdated software, no encryption – which made exfiltration easier once the person had access. The firm shut down in 2018 due to the reputational damage. The incident underscores that often the biggest “privacy breaches” can be for public interest – yet still devastating to those whose shady dealings were laid bare.

description: In Nov 2014, Sony Pictures Entertainment was hacked by a group calling itself “Guardians of Peace” (later U.S. officials attributed it to North Korea) in retaliation for a satirical film. The attackers crippled Sony’s network (wiping drives) and dumped a vast amount of sensitive data online: personal info and SSNs of ~6,000 employees, salaries of executives, entire private emails of top execs, unreleased films, and more – reportedly 100 terabytes of data. The leaks exposed embarrassing Hollywood emails (leading to firings), scripts, and sensitive employee and actor information. Sony’s ordeal was a wake-up call about destructive cyberattacks.
root_cause: Spear-phishing & malware: The attackers gained entry likely through a targeted phishing email or an exposed server password. Once in, they deployed malware (Destover wiper) to destroy systems and steal data. Sony’s IT lacked strong network segmentation, so the malware spread widely. North Korea was angry about The Interview film and sought revenge, making this a rare politically motivated corporate breach. Sony had to essentially rebuild its IT infrastructure. This incident highlighted nation-states’ willingness to attack private companies and the immense collateral privacy damage (employee data, personal correspondence) such attacks can cause.

description: In August 2014, a large cache of intimate photographs of female celebrities was posted on internet forums (notably 4chan and Reddit). Victims included Jennifer Lawrence, Kate Upton, and many others. It was dubbed “Celebgate” or “The Fappening.” How it happened: attackers obtained the celebrities’ Apple iCloud account credentials (likely via phishing or guessing security questions) and then downloaded their personal photos and videos. Over 500 private photos were leaked. This caused immense humiliation and privacy violation for the victims, and at least 4 hackers were later arrested and convicted.
root_cause: Credential hacking (phishing/guessing): Contrary to early speculation, Apple’s iCloud wasn’t broadly “breached” – instead, hackers specifically targeted celebrities’ accounts by guessing their password reset security questions or sending phishing emails to steal passwords. For example, one hacker admitted to phishing via fake Apple emails. Another used publicly known facts to answer security questions (e.g., a star’s birthplace or pet’s name). Once in, they accessed iCloud backups which often contained the camera roll. Apple responded by enabling alerts for iCloud downloads and urging two-factor authentication. This incident underlined the need for strong, unique passwords and 2FA – even (or especially) for high-profile individuals – and fundamentally that “the cloud” can be only as secure as the account-holder’s practices.

description: In 2015, the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) announced that its databases had been infiltrated by Chinese state hackers, constituting one of the worst breaches of U.S. government data. The personal records of ~21.5 million individuals were stolen, including 4.2 M federal employees and over 17 M people who had undergone background checks (e.g., for security clearances). The attackers got extremely sensitive data: personnel files, security clearance SF-86 forms (which detail an individual’s entire history, foreign contacts, mental health, etc.), and even 5.6 million fingerprints. The breach potentially compromised U.S. intelligence and counterintelligence operations and exposed millions to potential espionage or identity theft.
root_cause: State-sponsored hacking: Using a variant of the PlugX malware, likely via a phishing email to an OPM contractor, Chinese APT hackers established a foothold in 2014. OPM’s cyber defenses were weak (it had been warned repeatedly). The attackers gained administrator privileges, exfiltrating data undetected for months. Notably, they stole an OPM tech’s credentials (who had admin access) – possibly via a VPN token theft – to jump into the clearance database. The breach was discovered during an unrelated tool demo. This incident led to the resignation of the OPM director and a $133 M government credit monitoring program. It also spurred a major overhaul of federal cybersecurity (and encryption of data-at-rest for sensitive databases).

description: In Nov 2015, electronic toy maker VTech disclosed that its Learning Lodge app store and Kid Connect messaging platform were hacked. The breach exposed data on 6.4 million children and 4.9 million parents worldwide. Stolen info for kids included names, genders, and birthdates; for parents: names, email addresses, passwords, home addresses, and secret questions. In some cases, Kid Connect chat logs and profile photos of children were also exposed. No payment info was taken, but the incident was alarming as one of the first big IoT toy breaches, and because it violated children’s privacy (COPPA law issues).
root_cause: SQL injection & weak security: The hacker (who later came forward anonymously) used a simple SQL injection on VTech’s websites to dump the database. VTech had no encryption on passwords (stored in plaintext) and other glaring security lapses. The hacker said they didn’t intend to misuse the data and just wanted to highlight the flaws. The fallout: VTech was fined $650k by the FTC for violating COPPA (children’s privacy law) and forced to overhaul its security. This breach was a wake-up call about the safety of “smart toys” and prompted many companies to adopt stricter data protections for kid-focused products.

description: In Jun 2019, Canadian financial cooperative Desjardins announced an employee with legitimate access had maliciously collected and leaked information on 9.7 million individuals and businesses – the largest breach in Canadian banking history. Stolen data included names, addresses, birthdates, social insurance numbers (SINs), emails, and banking habits (like types of products held). The insider had been funneling data since 2017 to outside parties. The breach was discovered when police alerted Desjardins that a bundle of its customer info was found in a criminal investigation. This incident rocked trust in Canadian financial institutions and led to calls for stricter data safeguards and federal privacy law changes.
root_cause: Insider betrayal: A Desjardins call center employee, motivated by profit, gradually siphoned customer data over ~26 months. He saved data to USB drives and gave it to a contact who attempted to sell it. Red flags were missed – for example, he often queried the database without typical business reasons. After the breach, investigations cited Desjardins for inadequate access controls and monitoring. They’ve since implemented stricter measures (like tighter data export rules and behavioral analytics to spot unusual queries). This case underscores that internal threats can cause breaches equal in scale to external hacks, and sometimes only law enforcement can connect the dots if monitoring fails.
