description: In Oct 2019, LifeLabs – Canada’s largest medical testing lab – was hit by a cyberattack affecting data of 15 million patients (largely in Ontario and B.C.). Hackers obtained lab test results for 85,000 individuals and personal information (names, addresses, emails, logins, passwords, health card numbers) for millions. LifeLabs quietly paid a ransom (amount undisclosed) to secure the data, then revealed the breach publicly in Dec 2019. Provincial privacy commissioners later stated LifeLabs had inadequate safeguards and had broken privacy laws.
root_cause: Ransomware + extortion: Attackers likely gained entry via a known vulnerability or weak remote access and deployed ransomware, encrypting LifeLabs’ data and also exfiltrating copies. LifeLabs admitted to paying the ransom to retrieve data and prevent its leak. Technical details weren’t disclosed, but an independent review found outdated security (e.g., exposed servers, lack of network segmentation). The breach’s severity (medical data) and the ransom payoff provoked debate on cyberinsurance and breach disclosure. Regulators ordered LifeLabs to harden its IT and there’s a proposed class-action lawsuit. This case illustrates the grave risk ransomware poses to sensitive health information.

description: Between Aug and Sept 2018, British Airways’ website was compromised by a Magecart group. Around 380,000 booking transactions were skimmed, meaning customers’ credit card details (card numbers, expiration, CVV) and personal info entered on BA’s site were siphoned to the attackers. BA disclosed the breach quickly. No travel or passport info was taken, but the payment card theft led to fraudulent charges and card replacements. Under GDPR, the UK ICO investigated and initially fined BA £183 M (a record at the time) for failing to secure customer data (later reduced to £20 M).
root_cause: Digital supply-chain attack: Hackers compromised a third-party JavaScript library used by BA’s online payment page (or injected malicious code on BA’s site). Only 22 lines of extra code were added, but it real-time copied card details as customers entered them. BA’s security failed to detect this for two weeks. The incident emphasized the risk of third-party web scripts and the need for web app integrity control. It also was a landmark GDPR case, showing that even a client-side breach (no internal BA systems hacked) can result in major regulatory fines if preventative measures (like script subresource integrity or monitoring) were lacking.

description: In June 2018, attackers infiltrated Singapore’s largest health network, SingHealth, and stole records of 1.5 million patients – including the Prime Minister’s personal health data. The stolen data included names, National ID numbers, addresses, gender, race, date of birth, and outpatient visit info (diagnoses and doctors seen). Notably, the hackers specifically and repeatedly targeted PM Lee Hsien Loong’s records (likely seeking sensitive info). The breach, considered Singapore’s worst cyber attack, was attributed to a nation-state (suspected Chinese APT). It led to a major inquiry and stricter cyber laws (e.g., barring Internet access on government computers).
root_cause: Advanced persistent threat: The attackers gained initial access via a phishing email to an IT administrator at SingHealth’s specialist center. They then moved laterally over months. The attack succeeded due to several lapses: weak administrator passwords, an outdated patient database system, and IT staff who silenced security alarms that were firing. The post-breach report listed multiple “missed opportunities” to stop the hack. This breach underscored that even with relatively robust national cyber defenses, determined hackers can penetrate if internal vigilance falters. It also highlighted that medical data (even of a head of state) is a crown jewel target.

description: In Sept 2019, security researchers found an unsecured database hosted in Miami containing detailed information on virtually the entire population of Ecuador (~17 million people, plus some deceased – totaling ~20 M records). The data (18 GB) included full names, home addresses, dates of birth, national identification numbers (cedulas), tax identification numbers, employment information, phone numbers, and family relationships. Much of it seemed to come from government registries and an automotive association. The database was traced to an Ecuadorian marketing/data company named Novaestrat. The leak meant almost every Ecuadorian’s personal data was at risk of identity theft.
root_cause: Unsecured server: Novaestrat had aggregated data from various sources (some likely official) and stored it on an Elasticsearch server without any password. Essentially, anyone could query personal data of Ecuador’s citizens. The breach was discovered by researchers (vpnMentor) rather than malicious actors (as far as known). The Ecuadorian government reacted by arresting Novaestrat’s CEO and rushing to pass a long-pending data protection law. This incident showed the dangers of large-scale personal data aggregation by private firms in absence of strong privacy regulations, and it eerily illustrated what a “total information” breach of a nation looks like.
